prompt: Before the new index, why did the plan for a customer's last ten orders contain a `Sort`?
hint: What order does `orders_customer_id_idx` hand the rows over in?

choices.text: The index gives them by customer, not by time
choices.why: Right: the rows had to be ordered by placed_at afterwards to pick the newest ten.

choices.text: Because LIMIT always forces a sort, whatever the indexes
choices.why: After the new index the plan had a LIMIT and no Sort.

choices.text: The table was not vacuumed
choices.why: Vacuum does not change the order an index returns rows in.

choices.text: The planner chose it because the statistics were stale and it misjudged how many rows the customer had
choices.why: It estimated 11 and found 10; the sort was there because of the order, not a misestimate.

prompt: Why does the lesson run the before three times, thirty seconds each, instead of once?

choices.text: Because pgbench refuses runs shorter than ninety seconds
choices.why: It runs for whatever -T says.

choices.text: To see the noise
choices.why: Right: three runs of an unchanged database are three numbers, and their spread is the noise.

choices.text: To warm the cache before the index is built
choices.why: Warming is a side effect; the reason is to measure the spread.

choices.text: Because the tally only counts after three runs have finished
choices.why: The tally counts from the first call.

prompt: By the server's count, how many milliseconds per call did the new index save? Use the two means, 0.107 and 0.089.
After the index, the plan has no `Sort` and the execution went from 0.261 to 0.194 ms. What else changed in the plan?

choices.text: The scan stops at ten rows and touches 13 buffers instead of 16
choices.why: Right: the rows come out in order, so ten is enough.

choices.text: It reads the whole table
choices.why: It reads ten rows through the new index.

choices.text: It uses both indexes together in a bitmap
choices.why: It uses one Index Scan on the new index.

choices.text: It became a parallel plan
choices.why: No parallel workers appear.

prompt: The customer-orders latency ranged 0.836–0.857 ms before and 0.794–0.800 ms after. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: The change is real
choices.why: Right: the worst after is better than the best before.

choices.text: Nothing, because three runs prove nothing about any change
choices.why: Three runs whose ranges do not overlap are as close to proof as the rule allows.

choices.text: The change made it slower
choices.why: The after numbers are lower.

choices.text: The difference is noise, since it is under a millisecond
choices.why: Size is not the test; overlap with the run-to-run spread is.

prompt: The place-order latency was 8.156–8.794 ms before and 8.212–8.357 ms after. What may you say about the new index's cost on writes?

choices.text: It costs nothing on writes
choices.why: The measurement is too coarse to show it, which is different from showing it is zero.

choices.text: It made writes faster
choices.why: The after sits inside the before's range; nothing can be concluded.

choices.text: Not shown: the difference is smaller than the noise of these runs
choices.why: Right: a different measurement is needed, which the next section uses.

choices.text: It doubled the cost of each write, hidden by caching
choices.why: A doubling would be far outside the range.

prompt: Picking the before-run of 1134 transactions a second and the after-run of 1200, what percentage of extra throughput does the change appear to give? Round to the nearest whole number.
Put the lesson's rule for calling a change real in order.
items: Run the before at least three times
Run the after the same way, at least three times
Call it real only if they do not overlap
trap: The before has to exist before the change; the verdict needs both ranges.

prompt: The new index is 60 MB and the one on `customer_id` alone is 18 MB, though it adds only one 8-byte column. Why?
hint: How many orders does each customer have?

choices.text: The old index shares repeated values; the new keys are unique
choices.why: Right: a value that repeats is stored once with a list; customer and moment together never repeat.

choices.text: DESC indexes are stored twice
choices.why: A descending index is stored once, in the other order.

choices.text: Because timestamps are stored as long text strings
choices.why: timestamptz is 8 bytes of binary.

choices.text: Because the new index also holds total_cents and status for every order
choices.why: Only customer_id and placed_at are in it.

prompt: Where are the new index's 60 MB paid? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: On the disk
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In every backup
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In memory, competing with the tables
choices.why: Right: shared_buffers and the operating system's cache.

choices.text: In pg_stat_statements' table of statements
choices.why: The tally holds statements, not indexes.

prompt: Why does the lesson count "people" as a cost of an index?
hint: Lesson 11 found the result after three years.

choices.text: Each index needs a licence per developer
choices.why: PostgreSQL has no such licence.

choices.text: Because somebody has to rebuild every index by hand each night
choices.why: Indexes are maintained automatically as rows change.

choices.text: The next person must understand it before changing the table
choices.why: Right: an index with no record of why it exists is one nobody dares remove.

choices.text: Because users notice every new index on the screen
choices.why: Nobody sees an index on a screen.

prompt: Each person opening their order list saves 0.046 ms. Why does the lesson say nobody can see that?
hint: What delay can a person notice?

choices.text: It is two thousand times under what a person notices
choices.why: Right: people notice around a tenth of a second.

choices.text: Because the browser rounds all times to whole milliseconds
choices.why: Rounding is not the reason; the size is.

choices.text: The page is cached
choices.why: The workload's reads hit the database each time.

choices.text: Because pgbench measures something users never experience
choices.why: pgbench's latency is the closest thing to a user's wait this lab has.

prompt: A statement runs 200 times a second and a change saves it 0.5 ms a call. How many milliseconds of server time does it save per second?
The seller_id index saved about 870 ms of server time per second and the customer-orders index about 10 ms. Both were one `CREATE INDEX` line. What made the difference?

choices.text: The seller index is on a smaller table
choices.why: Both are on orders.

choices.text: The saving per call: 24 ms against 0.018
choices.why: Right: even at 36 calls a second against 575, the larger saving per call wins.

choices.text: The seller index was built first, so it got the memory
choices.why: Build order does not decide what an index saves.

choices.text: Because pg_stat_statements counts dashboards twice over
choices.why: Every statement is counted once per call.

prompt: In which version of this database would keeping the new index be the right decision?
hint: The arithmetic is the same; the numbers change.

choices.text: One where the customer's list tops the tally and the server is near the knee
choices.why: Right: then the saving is large in total and the processor time is scarce.

choices.text: Any version, since a faster query is always better
choices.why: The lesson's point is that faster is not automatically worth its cost.

choices.text: One with more disk free
choices.why: Disk is one cost; the benefit still has to be large enough.

choices.text: One where the tag search has already been fixed by lesson 8's index
choices.why: That makes the customer list relatively bigger, but not by itself worth 60 MB.

prompt: Why run `pg_get_indexdef` before dropping the index?

choices.text: To keep the exact statement that rebuilds it
choices.why: Right: an index dropped without its definition cannot be put back quickly.

choices.text: DROP INDEX refuses to run without it
choices.why: DROP INDEX needs nothing but the name.

choices.text: It frees the memory the index was using
choices.why: It only prints a definition.

choices.text: It makes the DROP happen concurrently, without blocking writes
choices.why: That is DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY.

prompt: The line of the change record people leave out, and the one that makes the result checkable, is the ___ line.
Match each line of the change record to what it holds.

pairs.right: the workload, the runs and the reset between them
the space and the extra work on writes
what was done, and the numbers it rests on

right_distractors: the name of whoever proposed it

prompt: Dropping the index took 76 ms with an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock. On a busy table, what does the lesson point to instead?

choices.text: Dropping it at night when no one is there to notice the lock
choices.why: Night is a schedule, not a way to avoid the lock.

choices.text: `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`
choices.why: Right: it does not block writes, at the price of taking longer.

choices.text: Truncating the table first
choices.why: That deletes every order.

choices.text: Restarting the server so that the lock is not needed
choices.why: A restart is an outage, not a way around a lock.

prompt: A colleague shows one before-run at 950 transactions a second and one after-run at 1010, and calls their index a 6% win. What do you ask for first?
hint: This lesson's own data had a 6% "win" between two runs.

choices.text: The index's size
choices.why: Cost matters, but first find out whether there is any gain.

choices.text: More runs of each, to compare the ranges
choices.why: Right: one run each cannot separate a gain from the noise.

choices.text: A bigger server, to see if the gain grows with it
choices.why: That changes two things at once.

choices.text: Nothing more: 6% is a large improvement for one index
choices.why: In this lesson two runs of the same database differed by 6%.
